y-m-34-01.title: If only two values are known, is the remainder determined?
y-m-34-01.topic: The roles of the remainder and the quotient: when dividing by a quadratic expression, is the remainder determined by the known values alone?
y-m-34-01.goal: Judge whether the remainder of a polynomial for which only some values are known is determined as one by comparing the number of unknowns with the number of known conditions, and make different polynomials that satisfy the same conditions to tell apart the roles of the quotient and remainder.
y-m-34-01.material:
For a polynomial f(x) with real coefficients, only the following two things are known.
  f(1)=3, f(2)=5
(The degree of f(x) and the coefficients of the remainder are not known.) Now you want to know the remainder when f(x) is divided by (x-1)(x-2).
y-m-34-01.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient (comparing the number of unknowns and conditions)
y-m-34-01.thinking.1: Making different examples that satisfy the conditions yourself
y-m-34-01.thinking.2: Telling apart what changes (the quotient) from what does not change (the remainder)
y-m-34-01.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-01.prereq.1: In polynomial division, (dividend)=(divisor)×(quotient)+(remainder), and the convention that the degree of the remainder is less than the degree of the divisor
y-m-34-01.prereq.2: Calculating the value of an expression by plugging a value of x into a polynomial
y-m-34-01.s.s1.prompt: Is the remainder when f(x) is divided by (x-1)(x-2) determined as one by these two values alone? Choose the most appropriate judgment.
y-m-34-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write the result of the division in the form f(x)=(divisor)×(quotient)+(remainder), and write what restriction the remainder has.
y-m-34-01.s.s1.hint.1: Count and compare how many unknowns are in the remainder and how many conditions are known.
y-m-34-01.s.s1.o.a: It is not determined. If the degree of f is not known, the quotient cannot be determined
y-m-34-01.s.s1.r.a: The remainder can be determined even without knowing the quotient. Start by counting how many unknowns there are in the remainder.
y-m-34-01.s.s1.o.b: It is not determined. One more value of x, such as f(0), must be known
y-m-34-01.s.s1.r.b: The number of values needed is decided by the number of unknowns in the expression for the remainder. First work out what form the remainder can be written in.
y-m-34-01.s.s1.o.c: It is determined. The remainder is of degree 1 or lower, so there are two unknowns and two conditions
y-m-34-01.s.s1.r.c: You counted the unknowns using the restriction on the degree of the remainder and compared with the number of known conditions.
y-m-34-01.s.s1.o.d: It is determined. The two known values f(1)=3 and f(2)=5 are themselves the remainder
y-m-34-01.s.s1.r.d: 3 and 5 are the values at x=1 and x=2. The remainder is an expression in x, so these values are not themselves the remainder.
y-m-34-01.s.s1.explain: In f(x)=(x-1)(x-2)Q(x)+R(x), the degree of R is less than 2, so you can write R(x)=ax+b. There are two unknowns, a and b, and plugging in x=1 and x=2 gives two different equations, a+b=3 and 2a+b=5, so a=2 and b=1 are determined. Even if the quotient Q is not determined, the remainder is determined.
y-m-34-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two different cubic expressions f(x)=x³+px²+qx+r (p, q, r are integers) that satisfy both f(1)=3 and f(2)=5.
y-m-34-01.s.s2.hint.0: Plug x=1 into f(1)=3 and x=2 into f(2)=5, and write the two equations that must hold among p, q, and r.
y-m-34-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose any one value of p, then calculate how q and r follow from the two equations.
y-m-34-01.s.s2.ok.c1: p, q, and r are all integers.
y-m-34-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose p, q, and r as integers.
y-m-34-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The value f(1) at x=1 is not 3.
y-m-34-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The value f(2) at x=2 is not 5.
y-m-34-01.s.s2.explain: For example, if p=0, then q=-5 and r=7, so f(x)=x³-5x+7, and f(1)=3 and f(2)=5. If p=1, f(x)=x³+x²-8x+9, and again f(1)=3 and f(2)=5. There are several f that satisfy the conditions like this.
y-m-34-01.s.s3.prompt: For the two f you just made, find and write the remainder when each is divided by (x-1)(x-2). Also explain whether the remainders are the same or different even though the f are different, and why.
y-m-34-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write f(x)=(x-1)(x-2)Q(x)+ax+b, plug in x=1 and x=2, and write the equations in a and b.
y-m-34-01.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the part that differs between the two f is the quotient or the remainder.
y-m-34-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Both f have the remainder 2x+1. This is because ...
y-m-34-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is there a reason you wrote the remainder in the form ax+b (degree 1 or lower)?
y-m-34-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say separately the part that changes when f changes (the quotient) and the part that does not change (the remainder)?
y-m-34-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you show the process by which f(1)=3 and f(2)=5 determine a and b?
y-m-34-01.s.s3.model.0: Both f have the remainder 2x+1. Writing f(x)=(x-1)(x-2)Q(x)+ax+b and plugging in x=1 and x=2 gives a+b=3 and 2a+b=5, so a=2 and b=1. Even if f is different, only the quotient Q changes, and the remainder is determined by the conditions on f(1) and f(2).
y-m-34-01.s.s3.model.1: x³-5x+7 has quotient x+3 and remainder 2x+1, and x³+x²-8x+9 has quotient x+4 and remainder 2x+1. The quotients differ but the remainders are the same because both satisfy the same conditions f(1)=3 and f(2)=5.

y-m-34-02.title: One line of the factoring solution went off
y-m-34-02.topic: Finding the error in a solution factoring a cubic expression using the factor theorem
y-m-34-02.goal: Find the sign error that arose in the link between the x that makes the value 0 and the form of the factor, choose a check value that surely reveals the error without expanding, and write the correct factorization.
y-m-34-02.material: A student's solution factoring the cubic expression f(x)=x³-2x²-5x+6 is below. The calculation written on each line is simple in itself.
y-m-34-02.thinking.0: Finding the location of the error line by line in the solution
y-m-34-02.thinking.1: Evaluating whether a checking method really reveals the error
y-m-34-02.thinking.2: Rewriting the error correctly and explaining the cause
y-m-34-02.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-02.prereq.1: Calculating the value of an expression by plugging a value of x into a polynomial
y-m-34-02.prereq.2: Basic experience with factoring that writes a polynomial as a product of linear expressions
y-m-34-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in this solution that went off.
y-m-34-02.s.s1.hint.0: Redo the calculation of each line yourself, and check separately the line that moves from 'the value is 0' to 'the factor is something'.
y-m-34-02.s.s1.hint.1: Actually expand the result of the last line and compare it with f(x), and if it does not match, trace back to see which factor is suspicious.
y-m-34-02.s.s1.line.0: Look for factor candidates among the divisors of the constant term 6, ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6.
y-m-34-02.s.s1.line.1: f(1)=1-2-5+6=0, so x-1 is a factor.
y-m-34-02.s.s1.line.2: f(3)=27-18-15+6=0, so x+3 is also a factor.
y-m-34-02.s.s1.line.3: f(-2)=-8-8+10+6=0, so x+2 is also a factor.
y-m-34-02.s.s1.explain: The 3rd line went off. The calculation f(3)=0 is right, but when the x that makes the value 0 is 3, the factor is x-3, not x+3 (the x that makes x-3=0 is 3). So the result in the 5th line is also wrong. In fact, expanding (x-1)(x+3)(x+2) gives x³+4x²+x-6. The calculations in lines 1, 2, and 4 are all right. If you chose the 5th line, trace back to the 3rd line to see why that result was wrong.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to show surely, with only one check and without expanding, that the result of the 5th line (x-1)(x+3)(x+2)=f(x) is wrong. Choose all the checks that surely reveal the mismatch.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.hint.0: For each check, calculate the values of f(x) and of (x-1)(x+3)(x+2) and compare them.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.hint.1: Look at what the comparison gives at the x values that were already used in the solution to decide the factors.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.o.a: Plug x=-2 into both sides and compare
y-m-34-02.s.s2.r.a: x=-2 is a value the solution already confirmed makes the value of f 0. At this value both sides are 0, so the mismatch does not show.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.o.b: Plug x=3 into both sides and compare
y-m-34-02.s.s2.r.b: At x=3, f is 0 but (x-1)(x+3)(x+2) is 60. This is a check that found a place where the values of the two sides differ.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.o.c: Compare the coefficients of the leading term
y-m-34-02.s.s2.r.c: Both sides have 1 as the coefficient of x³, so they are the same. This is a check that both the right solution and the wrong solution pass.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.o.d: Plug x=1 into both sides and compare
y-m-34-02.s.s2.r.d: x=1 is also a value already used to decide a factor, so both sides are 0. Passing does not guarantee it is right.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.o.e: Plug x=0 into both sides and compare
y-m-34-02.s.s2.r.e: At x=0, f is 6 but (x-1)(x+3)(x+2) is -6. This is a check that reveals the sign of the constant term is off.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.explain: x=1 and x=-2 are values already used when deciding the factors in the solution, so both sides are 0, and the leading coefficient is 1 on both sides. Such checks let a wrong result pass too. At x=0, f(0)=6 and (0-1)(0+3)(0+2)=-6, and at x=3, f(3)=0 and 2·6·5=60, so they mismatch. A check that the values are the same may mean not 'it is not wrong' but 'we still don't know from this value'.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.acc.0: The x=3 check alone reveals the mismatch. It is even better if you also see that there are other values such as x=0.
y-m-34-02.s.s2.acc.1: The x=0 check alone reveals the mismatch. It is even better if you also see that there are other values such as x=3.
y-m-34-02.s.s3.prompt: Write the correct factorization, and explain in one or two sentences which part of the solution was thought about wrongly and how.
y-m-34-02.s.s3.hint.0: When f(3)=0, write yourself what linear expression becomes 0 when 3 is plugged in for x.
y-m-34-02.s.s3.hint.1: Plug the corrected result into x=0 and check whether it matches f(0)=6.
y-m-34-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: f(x)=... The part I thought about wrongly is ...
y-m-34-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the corrected result confirmed with x=0 or the like?
y-m-34-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write in your own words the link 'if the x that makes the value 0 is a, the factor is x-a'?
y-m-34-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you point to the cause as a misunderstanding of how the sign connects, not just a simple 'mistake'?
y-m-34-02.s.s3.model.0: f(x)=(x-1)(x-3)(x+2). If f(3)=0, the factor is x-3, not x+3, but I wrote the sign the opposite way.
y-m-34-02.s.s3.model.1: It is (x+2)(x-1)(x-3). In the factor theorem, if f(a)=0 then x-a is a factor, so if f(3)=0 then x-3 is a factor, but I wrongly wrote x+3.

y-m-34-03.title: How many values of x does it need to hold for to be enough?
y-m-34-03.topic: Identity: how many x values must it hold for to be settled as holding for all x?
y-m-34-03.goal: Say how your confidence in judging an identity should change as the evidence from checking values one at a time grows, and judge how the number of values needed is connected to the degree of the polynomial.
y-m-34-03.material: a, b, and c are constants, and there is an equation ax²+bx+c=0 in x. You are told one at a time for which values of x this equation holds. At each step, choose whether you may judge it to be an equation that holds for all x (an identity).
y-m-34-03.thinking.0: Adjusting your judgment and confidence as evidence builds up
y-m-34-03.thinking.1: Understanding why holding at one or two values cannot be a proof
y-m-34-03.thinking.2: Generalizing the relationship between the number of values needed and the degree
y-m-34-03.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-03.prereq.1: The difference between an identity and an equation for polynomials (an equation that holds for all x versus one that holds only for particular x)
y-m-34-03.prereq.2: The form of an expression of degree 2 or lower, ax²+bx+c
y-m-34-03.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Choose your judgment each time.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write side by side 'how many values have been checked so far' and 'what the degree of the expression is'.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.hint.1: Choose a, b, and c yourself (for example, so that the equation holds at x=1) and test whether it holds at other x too.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Plugging in x=1, the equation holds.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can we judge that this equation is an identity?
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.after: Holding at one value makes it hard to say either that it is an identity or that it is not. For example, if a=1, b=-3, c=2, it holds at x=1, but at x=0 it becomes 2=0, so it does not hold.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is an identity. Because the equation held at the value I plugged in
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Holding at one value happens in the same way when that value is a root of the equation. We do not yet know whether it holds at other values.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is too early to say for sure. That value might be a root
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: It holds even if one value is a root. This judgment considered whether the number of values checked is enough for the judgment.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is not an identity. Because it was confirmed at only one value
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You did not confirm that it fails at the values you did not check. There is not yet any basis to say 'it is not' either.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.after: If a=1, b=-3, c=2, it holds at both x=1 and x=2 but not at x=0. Even with two values confirmed, you cannot yet be sure. The judgment stays the same, but it has become a little clearer what shape an expression that could be a counterexample has.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is an identity. Because it held at two different values
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Two values could also be the two roots of a quadratic expression. Recall that a quadratic expression can have two roots.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Not yet known. A quadratic expression can have two roots
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You judged by comparing the number of values checked with the possible number of roots.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is not an identity. Because it holds for only two values
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: It has not yet been confirmed that it holds for only two values. That two values were checked is different from it holding for only two values.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.after: If an expression of degree 2 or lower is not 0, it has at most two roots. If it holds at three different values, then a=b=c=0 and it holds for all x. This time the evidence was enough to change the judgment.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Not yet known. We need to check up to a fourth value
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Checking more does no harm, but this expression has the condition that it is of degree 2 or lower, so three values exceed the number of roots.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It is not an identity. Because it held at only three values
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Holding at three values is not evidence against it. Think about what happens when an expression of degree 2 or lower is 0 at three different values.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is an identity. An expression of degree 2 or lower cannot have three roots
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You drew the conclusion by comparing the degree of the expression with the number of values checked.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.reflect: How did your judgment change over the three steps, and what caused that change? If the same three values had been confirmed but the expression had been a quartic ax⁴+bx³+cx²+dx+e=0, how should the judgment differ?
y-m-34-03.s.s2.prompt: If a polynomial P(x) in x of degree 4 or lower is 0 at how many different values of x can we settle that P(x) is 0 for all x? Choose the smallest number that lets us settle it.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think about the maximum number of different roots a quartic expression can have.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.hint.1: Count at how many values of x an expression such as x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3) is 0.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.r.a: x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3) is 0 at four different values but is not 0 for all x. A quartic expression can have four roots.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.r.b: If a polynomial of degree 4 has 5 roots, it becomes the zero polynomial. This judgment applied the rule 'degree + 1'.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.r.c: With 6 it is settled, but it is not the smallest number. It is already settled with 5.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.r.d: 3 is not enough. A quartic expression can have up to four roots.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.explain: If a polynomial of degree n or lower is not 0, it has at most n different roots. So if it is 0 at n+1 different values, all its coefficients are 0 and it holds for all x. For degree 4 or lower it is 5. The 3 for an expression of degree 2 or lower earlier follows the same rule.

y-m-34-04.title: The sum of cubes of two numbers whose sum is 5
y-m-34-04.topic: Multiplication formulas and the sum and product of two letters: the sum of cubes when only the sum is known
y-m-34-04.goal: Judge step by step whether the value of a³+b³ is determined when only the sum is known and when both the sum and product are known, and check the judgment yourself with examples that have the same sum but different sums of cubes.
y-m-34-04.material: For two numbers a and b, it is known that a+b=5. You want to know the value of a³+b³ (a³ is the number you get by multiplying a three times). Look at how your judgment changes as the known information increases one piece at a time.
y-m-34-04.thinking.0: Revising your judgment as the known information increases
y-m-34-04.thinking.1: Showing with counterexamples that it 'is not determined'
y-m-34-04.thinking.2: Finding the information needed using the multiplication formula
y-m-34-04.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-04.prereq.1: Able to calculate the multiplication formula that expands (a+b)³, or its expanded result, directly
y-m-34-04.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Choose your judgment each time.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write whether, with what is known so far, you can choose a and b in different ways, and if so, how many ways there are.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.hint.1: Choose two or three pairs with sum 5, calculate a³+b³ directly for each, and compare.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you judge about the value of a³+b³?
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Having the same sum does not guarantee that the sum of cubes is the same too. You can check by making just two concrete pairs and comparing.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The sum is known to be 5, so a³+b³ is 5³=125
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: It generally does not hold that the sum of cubes of two numbers with sum 5 is the cube of 5. Expanding (a+b)³ has other terms too.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Not yet known. We need to choose a and b differently and compare the values
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is the thinking of making different pairs with the same sum and comparing them.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is not determined. There are two letters but only one equation
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The conclusion is right, but you cannot always judge just by counting the number of letters and equations. Making one example to check makes it more certain.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.info: It is also known that a and b are both integers.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now is a³+b³ determined as one value?
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Even with the integer condition, there are several pairs with sum 5. The new information did not change the judgment, but it narrowed the range of possible cases to integer pairs. Let's check this ourselves below.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is determined. With the integer condition, a and b are determined as one
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Integer pairs with sum 5 keep going, such as (1,4), (2,3), (0,5), (-1,6). The integer condition alone does not reduce them to one.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It may not be determined. There are several integer pairs with sum 5
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Although a condition was added, you directly examined the possibilities that remain and kept your judgment.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is determined. They are integers, so we can find a and b right away
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: With the single equation a+b=5, a and b are not determined as one either.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the value of a³+b³?
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.after: (a+b)³=a³+b³+3ab(a+b), so a³+b³=125-3·4·5=65. Calculating with a=1, b=4 also gives 1+64=65, the same. When both the sum and product are known, it is determined.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: In (a+b)³=a³+b³+3ab(a+b), this subtracted only 12 for 3ab without multiplying by (a+b).
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This was found by subtracting 3ab(a+b)=3·4·5=60 from the expansion of (a+b)³.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This still used only the sum and did not use the information about the product.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This subtracted ab(a+b)=20 instead of 3ab(a+b). The coefficient 3 was left out.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.reflect: Over the three steps, what information made you change your judgment and what information did not? If it were a²+b² instead of a³+b³, would the sum alone determine it, or would the product also be needed?
y-m-34-04.s.s2.prompt: Make three integer pairs a, b with a+b=5 whose values of a³+b³ are all different. (Pairs that differ only in order count as the same pair.)
y-m-34-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write how b is determined once you fix a, and make a table of a few pairs.
y-m-34-04.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate a³+b³ for each pair and pick the pairs that give different values.
y-m-34-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose a and b as integers.
y-m-34-04.s.s2.explain: (1,4) gives 1+64=65, (2,3) gives 8+27=35, (0,5) gives 125, and (-1,6) gives -1+216=215. The sums are all 5, but the sums of cubes differ. Since a³+b³=125-15ab, if ab differs, the value differs too.

y-m-34-05.title: If the equation is right, is it accepted as the quotient and remainder?
y-m-34-05.topic: Polynomial division: the condition for being the quotient and remainder even when A=BQ+R holds
y-m-34-05.goal: Confirm yourself that there are several (Q,R) for which A=B·Q+R holds, understand that a condition on the degree of the remainder is needed to accept them as the quotient and remainder, and continue the division by fixing an answer that does not fit the condition.
y-m-34-05.material:
Divide A(x)=x³+2x²+3x+4 by B(x)=x²+1. Three students said the following, and all three confirmed that 'A=B·Q+R holds'.
  Jimin: quotient Q=x+2, remainder R=2x+2
  Harin: quotient Q=x+1, remainder R=x²+2x+3
  Doyun: quotient Q=x, remainder R=2x²+2x+4
y-m-34-05.thinking.0: Telling apart the identity of the expression from the conditions on the result of a division
y-m-34-05.thinking.1: Constructing several solutions and discovering that uniqueness comes from a convention
y-m-34-05.thinking.2: Continuing from a wrong answer to a right answer
y-m-34-05.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-05.prereq.1: Expanding products of polynomials and adding and subtracting them
y-m-34-05.prereq.2: The degree of a polynomial (the degree of the highest term)
y-m-34-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write Q=x+p and expand B·Q. If you subtract that result from A, it should become R.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.var.u: Coefficient u of x² in R
y-m-34-05.s.s1.var.v: Coefficient v of x in R
y-m-34-05.s.s1.fail.c1: Please choose p, u, v, and w as integers.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.ok.c2: The coefficient of the x² term matches A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.fail.c2: When B·Q+R is expanded, the coefficient of the x² term differs from the 2 in A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.ok.c3: The coefficient of the x term matches A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.fail.c3: When B·Q+R is expanded, the coefficient of the x term differs from the 3 in A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.fail.c4: When B·Q+R is expanded, the constant term differs from the 4 in A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.explain: B·(x+p)=x³+px²+x+p, so R=A-B·Q=(2-p)x²+2x+(4-p). p=2 is Jimin's answer, p=1 is Harin's answer, p=0 is Doyun's answer, and there are as many more as you like, such as p=3 or p=-1.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.prompt: Even though there are several pairs (Q,R) like this, what convention is needed to speak of 'the quotient and remainder of the division' as one?
y-m-34-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put the pairs made above side by side and compare what differs from pair to pair in Q and R.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.hint.1: Apply each convention in the options to the pairs above and count how many pairs remain.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.o.a: Only the pair with the lowest degree of Q should be accepted
y-m-34-05.s.s2.r.a: The Q of the pairs you made are all linear. This convention filters out no pair.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.o.d: Only pairs in which all coefficients of R are integers should be accepted
y-m-34-05.s.s2.r.d: The pairs you made all have integer coefficients, so this convention filters nothing out.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.explain: With the convention that the degree of R must be less than the degree of B (2), the coefficient of x² must be 0, so p=2, that is, Q=x+2, R=2x+2 is the only one that remains. Without this convention, there are as many pairs as you like for which the equation holds. So when we state the result of a division, we also say 'the degree of the remainder is less than the degree of the divisor'.
y-m-34-05.s.s3.prompt: Harin said Q=x+1, R=x²+2x+3. The equation is right, so explain why it is hard to accept it as the 'result of the division', and show the path from Harin's R to Jimin's answer.
y-m-34-05.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the degree of Harin's R with the degree of the divisor B.
y-m-34-05.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate what the quotient and remainder become if you divide Harin's R by B once more.
y-m-34-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The degree of Harin's R is ..., so ...
y-m-34-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you point out that the degree of R is not less than the degree of B?
y-m-34-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the result of dividing R by B once more (quotient 1, remainder 2x+2)?
y-m-34-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you combine that result to reach Jimin's answer Q=x+2, R=2x+2?
y-m-34-05.s.s3.model.0: The degree of R=x²+2x+3 is 2, so it is not less than the degree of the divisor x²+1. It can still be divided further. x²+2x+3=(x²+1)·1+(2x+2), so adding 1 to the quotient gives x+2, and the remainder is 2x+2.
y-m-34-05.s.s3.model.1: If the remainder is a quadratic expression, it can be divided once more by the divisor, so it is not finished yet. Dividing R by x²+1 gives quotient 1 and remainder 2x+2, and the total quotient is x+1+1=x+2, the same as Jimin's answer.

y-m-34-06.title: Possible b in a quadratic expression with constant term 12
y-m-34-06.topic: Factoring quadratic expressions: possible coefficients of the linear term when the constant term is 12
y-m-34-06.goal: Check what cases the conclusion 'we found them all' left out, and find several integers b that satisfy the condition and a way to collect them without leaving any out.
y-m-34-06.material: For an integer b, you want to find all values of b for which the quadratic expression x²+bx+12 can be written as a product of two linear expressions with integer coefficients, (x+p)(x+q). A student summarized it as below.
y-m-34-06.thinking.0: Finding the cases that were left out and pointing out the error of generalizing
y-m-34-06.thinking.1: Systematically constructing several answers that satisfy the restriction
y-m-34-06.thinking.2: Explaining the reason for the impossible cases
y-m-34-06.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-06.prereq.1: The relationship between product and sum when a quadratic expression x²+bx+c is written as (x+p)(x+q)
y-m-34-06.s.s1.prompt: Pick the one line in this summary that is hard to believe.
y-m-34-06.s.s1.line.0: Writing x²+bx+12=(x+p)(x+q), we have pq=12 and p+q=b.
y-m-34-06.s.s1.line.1: The pairs of positive integers with pq=12 are (1,12), (2,6), (3,4).
y-m-34-06.s.s1.line.2: Therefore it can be factored when b=13, 8, 7.
y-m-34-06.s.s1.line.3: These three pairs are the only ones, so the possible b are only the three, 7, 8, 13.
y-m-34-06.s.s1.explain: The 4th line is the problem. Lines 1 to 3 are right. But in the 2nd line p and q were limited to only 'positive integers', whereas if pq=12, p and q may both be negative. For example, (-3)(-4)=12 and p+q=-7, so b=-7 is also possible. 'These three pairs are the only ones' is a conclusion that did not check for cases left out.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter four different integers b for which x²+bx+12 can be written as a product of two linear expressions with integer coefficients.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.hint.0: Make a table of integer pairs p, q whose product is 12, calculate the sum p+q of each pair, and write it as b.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many different sums appear in the table. If there are fewer than four, check whether any pairs were left out.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.var.b: Coefficient b of the linear term
y-m-34-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose b as an integer.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.ok.c2: With this b, there may be two numbers whose product is 12 and whose sum is b.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.fail.c2: With this b, you cannot find two real numbers whose product is 12 and whose sum is b.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.ok.c3: There are two integers whose product is 12 and whose sum is b.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.fail.c3: With this b, you cannot find two integers whose product is 12 and whose sum is b.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.explain: The integer pairs with product 12 are (1,12), (2,6), (3,4) and (-1,-12), (-2,-6), (-3,-4). The sums are 13, 8, 7, -13, -8, -7, so the possible b are six in all (±7, ±8, ±13).
y-m-34-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one integer b that is not in the list you found, and explain why it cannot be factored with integer coefficients.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write candidates and check whether there are two integers with product 12 that have that b as their sum.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare with the list of all possible values of the sums of pairs with product 12.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: b=5 doesn't work. This is because ...
y-m-34-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is the b you picked really a value not in the list?
y-m-34-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you give the reason by using the two conditions, sum and product, together, or by the discriminant?
y-m-34-06.s.s2.because.model.0: b=5 doesn't work. The sum of two integers with product 12 is only ±7, ±8, ±13, so it cannot be 5.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.because.model.1: If b=6, then in x²+6x+12 we have b²-4·12=36-48<0, so there is no real root and it cannot be factored.

y-m-34-07.title: If a³+b³+c³=3abc, are the three numbers equal?
y-m-34-07.topic: Multiplication formulas: must the three numbers be equal in a³+b³+c³=3abc?
y-m-34-07.goal: Decide with counterexamples whether the claim 'if the equation holds, the three numbers are equal' is true or false, and examine what extra condition makes the claim true.
y-m-34-07.material:
For real numbers a, b, c, a student made the following claim.
  Claim: If a³+b³+c³=3abc, then a=b=c.
The student checked with a=b=c=2. Since 8+8+8=24=3·8, the equation holds. ('3abc' means 3 times a times b times c.)
y-m-34-07.thinking.0: Telling apart the direction of a claim (condition and conclusion)
y-m-34-07.thinking.2: Finding the condition under which the claim holds
y-m-34-07.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-07.prereq.1: You do not need to have memorized the factorization of a³+b³+c³-3abc, but you can read its meaning when you see the factored expression
y-m-34-07.prereq.2: Cubes of real numbers and calculations with negative numbers
y-m-34-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most appropriate judgment about this claim.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.hint.0: Put into words which direction the student checked: 'if the equation holds, the three numbers are equal' or 'if the three numbers are equal, the equation holds'.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.hint.1: Test a few times with small integers whether there are cases where the equation holds but the three numbers are not equal. Plug in negative numbers too.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.o.a: It is true. Because we confirmed that the equation holds when a=b=c
y-m-34-07.s.s1.r.a: What was checked is the direction 'if the three numbers are equal, the equation holds'. The claim is the opposite direction.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.o.b: It is true. The expression stays the same when a, b, c are swapped, so the three numbers must be equal
y-m-34-07.s.s1.r.b: An expression staying the same when you swap the letters (symmetry) does not mean the three numbers must be equal.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.o.c: It is false. If the numbers are not all positive, the equation does not hold
y-m-34-07.s.s1.r.c: This asserted it without actually plugging in cases that include negative numbers.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.o.d: Not yet known. We look for cases where the three numbers differ but the equation holds
y-m-34-07.s.s1.r.d: You chose the method of looking for yourself whether there are cases that break the claim.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.explain: The claim says 'always', so checking one direction (if the three numbers are equal, the equation holds) is not enough, and you need to test whether there is an example where the equation holds but the three numbers are not equal. If you test, a counterexample like (1, 2, -3) turns up.
y-m-34-07.s.s2.prompt: Make three different real triples (a, b, c) that satisfy the equation a³+b³+c³=3abc but whose a, b, c are not all equal. (Using small integers is convenient.)
y-m-34-07.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a few small integers and calculate a³+b³+c³ and 3abc separately and compare. Plug in negative numbers too.
y-m-34-07.s.s2.hint.1: When an example where the equation holds turns up, calculate the value of a+b+c in that example and compare it with other examples.
y-m-34-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The three numbers are not all equal.
y-m-34-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The three numbers are all equal. To be a counterexample, they must be different from each other.
y-m-34-07.s.s2.explain: (1, 2, -3): 1+8-27=-18 and 3·1·2·(-3)=-18, so they are equal. In the examples you made, the sum of the three numbers is always 0. Since a³+b³+c³-3abc=(a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²-ab-bc-ca), if a+b+c=0 the equation holds even when the three numbers are different.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.prompt: What condition could be added to make the claim 'if the equation holds, a=b=c' true? Choose all the conditions that, when added, necessarily make a=b=c.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.hint.0: In the form where a³+b³+c³-3abc is written as a product of (a+b+c) and another factor, split up what value each factor must have for the product to be 0.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.hint.1: For the condition in each option, test with the examples you made above whether there is an example where the condition is satisfied and the equation holds.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.o.a: a, b, and c are all integers
y-m-34-07.s.s3.r.a: (1, 2, -3) is a counterexample that is all integers and satisfies the equation.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.o.b: a, b, and c are all positive
y-m-34-07.s.s3.r.b: If they are positive, the sum cannot be 0, so the other factor is 0 and the three numbers become equal.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.r.c: In (1, 2, -3), abc=-6 and yet the three numbers are not equal.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.r.d: If the sum is not 0, the remaining factor must be 0, and then the three numbers become equal.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.o.e: a, b, and c are all negative
y-m-34-07.s.s3.r.e: The sum of negative numbers cannot be 0 either, so for the same reason as with the positive case, the three numbers become equal.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.explain: a³+b³+c³-3abc=(1/2)(a+b+c)·{(a-b)²+(b-c)²+(c-a)²}. If a+b+c≠0, then when the equation holds the second factor must be 0, and then a=b=c. If all are positive or all are negative, the sum is not 0, so this works. The condition that they are integers or abc≠0 does not stop (1, 2, -3).
y-m-34-07.s.s3.acc.0: Both conditions are right. But it would be good to also see that there is a wider condition, that the sum is not 0.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.acc.1: You chose the widest condition. It would be even better to see that the positive or negative conditions also guarantee the sum is not 0 and so reach the same conclusion.

y-m-34-08.title: Choosing a way to expand the product of four linear expressions
y-m-34-08.topic: Multiplication formulas and substitution: comparing ways of pairing up and expanding the product of four linear expressions
y-m-34-08.goal: Compare three ways of grouping four linear expressions in pairs, choose the grouping that creates a common part, and check with examples you make yourself the condition under which that method works, and sum it up in words.
y-m-34-08.material: You want to expand (x+1)(x+2)(x+3)(x+4). One way is to group the four linear expressions in pairs and multiply those first. There are three ways of grouping in all.
y-m-34-08.thinking.0: Comparing the efficiency of several strategies
y-m-34-08.thinking.1: Making new examples that satisfy a condition
y-m-34-08.thinking.2: Generalizing the condition under which a strategy works
y-m-34-08.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-08.prereq.1: Multiplying linear expressions and expanding into a quadratic expression
y-m-34-08.prereq.2: Experience calculating by replacing a chunk of an expression with one letter (substitution)
y-m-34-08.s.s1.prompt: Multiplying in pairs makes two quadratic expressions. Which grouping makes the coefficients of x in the two quadratic expressions equal, so that you can treat x²+(some number)x as one chunk and calculate?
y-m-34-08.s.s1.hint.0: For each of the three groupings, expand the two quadratic expressions and write the coefficients of x side by side.
y-m-34-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether there is a grouping in which the coefficients of x are equal.
y-m-34-08.s.s1.r.a: You chose it by expanding each grouping and finding the case where the coefficients of x are equal.
y-m-34-08.s.s1.r.b: Expanding gives x²+3x+2 and x²+7x+12, so the coefficients of x differ. No chunk is formed.
y-m-34-08.s.s1.r.c: Expanding gives x²+4x+3 and x²+6x+8, so the coefficients of x differ.
y-m-34-08.s.s1.o.d: The coefficients of x become equal whichever grouping you multiply
y-m-34-08.s.s1.r.d: This judgment did not expand the three groupings and compare the coefficients of x. Compare them directly.
y-m-34-08.s.s1.explain: (x+1)(x+4)=x²+5x+4 and (x+2)(x+3)=x²+5x+6, so the coefficients of x are equal. Letting x²+5x=t gives (t+4)(t+6)=t²+10t+24, and changing t back gives x⁴+10x³+35x²+50x+24. The other two groupings have different coefficients of x, so this method does not work for them.
y-m-34-08.s.s2.prompt: In (x+a)(x+b)(x+c)(x+d) (integers with 1≤a<b<c<d≤9), make three different (a, b, c, d) for which the coefficients of x in the two quadratic expressions become equal when you group a with d and b with c. (Exclude 1, 2, 3, 4.)
y-m-34-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write the coefficients of x in letters when (x+a)(x+d) and (x+b)(x+c) are expanded.
y-m-34-08.s.s2.hint.1: Try a few small numbers and collect in a table the cases where the two coefficients are equal.
y-m-34-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose a, b, c, d as integers from 1 to 9.
y-m-34-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The coefficients of x in (x+a)(x+d) and (x+b)(x+c) are equal.
y-m-34-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The coefficients of x in (x+a)(x+d) and (x+b)(x+c) are different from each other.
y-m-34-08.s.s2.fail.c4: 1, 2, 3, 4 is an example already seen. Please make one with other numbers.
y-m-34-08.s.s2.explain: For example, (1, 3, 4, 6): (x+1)(x+6)=x²+7x+6 and (x+3)(x+4)=x²+7x+12, so the coefficients of x are equal. This grouping works when the sum of the smallest and largest numbers equals the sum of the middle two numbers.
y-m-34-08.s.s3.prompt: State the condition under which this grouping works as a relationship among the four constants, and write the result of expanding (x+1)(x+2)(x+3)(x+4) with that method.
y-m-34-08.s.s3.hint.0: In the examples you made above, calculate and compare the sum of each of the two pairs you grouped.
y-m-34-08.s.s3.hint.1: Replace x²+5x with one letter, expand (t+4)(t+6), and then change back.
y-m-34-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The condition under which the grouping works is ..., and expanding gives ...
y-m-34-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you state the condition as a relationship among the constants (the sums of the two pairs are equal)?
y-m-34-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is each coefficient of the expanded result right? Did you compare with another method (multiplying one at a time)?
y-m-34-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say why you replaced x²+5x with one letter?
y-m-34-08.s.s3.model.0: It works when the sum of the smallest and largest numbers equals the sum of the middle two numbers (1+4=2+3). Letting x²+5x=t gives (t+4)(t+6)=t²+10t+24, so the result is x⁴+10x³+35x²+50x+24.
y-m-34-08.s.s3.model.1: If the sums of the two grouped pairs are equal (1+4=2+3=5), the coefficients of x are equal. So expanding (x²+5x+4)(x²+5x+6) gives x⁴+10x³+35x²+50x+24.

y-m-34-09.title: What degree can the sum of two cubic expressions be?
y-m-34-09.topic: How the degree changes in addition and multiplication of polynomials
y-m-34-09.goal: Sort out all the degrees the sum of two cubic expressions can have, construct examples that are exactly a linear expression according to conditions, and explain why the degree of a product does not drop, unlike a sum.
y-m-34-09.material: A and B are both cubic expressions with integer coefficients (expressions whose leading-term coefficient of x³ is not 0). The case where A+B is 0 (the expression with all coefficients 0) does not have a degree to speak of, so we do not consider it.
y-m-34-09.thinking.0: Considering all possible cases without missing any
y-m-34-09.thinking.1: Constructing several examples that satisfy a restriction
y-m-34-09.thinking.2: Explaining by comparing the degrees of the sum and the product
y-m-34-09.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-09.prereq.1: The meaning of the degree and the leading term of a polynomial
y-m-34-09.s.s1.prompt: When A+B is not 0, choose all the possible degrees of A+B.
y-m-34-09.s.s1.hint.0: Choose two cubic expressions yourself, calculate the sum, and write its degree, and do this several times. Also vary what value the sum of the two leading coefficients takes.
y-m-34-09.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether there are cases where the degree gets higher in a sum, and what the highest degree can never exceed.
y-m-34-09.s.s1.r.a: In a sum, degrees do not add. Degrees adding is something that happens in a product.
y-m-34-09.s.s1.r.b: If the leading terms add up and disappear and an x² term remains, it is a quadratic expression.
y-m-34-09.s.s1.r.c: If the x³, x², and x terms all disappear and only the constant remains, it is degree 0.
y-m-34-09.s.s1.r.d: In a sum, a term higher than the higher degree of the two expressions cannot newly appear.
y-m-34-09.s.s1.r.e: If the sum of the leading coefficients is not 0, it is a cubic expression.
y-m-34-09.s.s1.r.f: If the x³ and x² terms disappear and an x term remains, it is a linear expression.
y-m-34-09.s.s1.explain: The leading term of the sum is x³ or lower. If the sum of the x³ coefficients is not 0, the degree is 3; if that sum is 0 and an x² term remains, the degree is 2; if an x term remains, 1; if only the constant remains, 0 (for example, the sum of x³+1 and -x³ is 1). Degree 4 or 6 cannot occur.
y-m-34-09.s.s2.prompt: A(x)=2x³-x²+4x+1. Make three different cubic expressions B(x)=px³+qx²+rx+s (p, q, r, s are integers) such that A+B is exactly a linear expression.
y-m-34-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write each coefficient of A+B as (coefficient of A)+(coefficient of B).
y-m-34-09.s.s2.hint.1: The coefficients of the degree 3 and degree 2 terms must be 0, and the coefficient of the degree 1 term must not be 0. Write one condition for each coefficient and turn them into equations in p, q, r, and s.
y-m-34-09.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose p, q, r, s as integers.
y-m-34-09.s.s2.fail.c2: B must be a cubic expression. The coefficient of x³ must not be 0.
y-m-34-09.s.s2.ok.c3: The x³ and x² terms of A+B have disappeared.
y-m-34-09.s.s2.fail.c3: An x³ or x² term remains in A+B.
y-m-34-09.s.s2.ok.c4: The x term of A+B remains, so it is a linear expression.
y-m-34-09.s.s2.fail.c4: The x term of A+B has also disappeared, so it is not a linear expression.
y-m-34-09.s.s2.explain: A+B=(2+p)x³+(-1+q)x²+(4+r)x+(1+s), so p=-2 and q=1, r is not -4, and s can be any integer. For example, if B=-2x³+x²+x+5, then A+B=5x+6.
y-m-34-09.s.s3.prompt: When A and B are both cubic expressions, the degree of A·B is always 6. Explain why the degree of a product does not drop, unlike the sum A+B.
y-m-34-09.s.s3.hint.0: Write A=ax³+... and B=bx³+..., and write how the term of the highest degree in A·B is made.
y-m-34-09.s.s3.hint.1: Recall what disappeared in the example where the degree dropped in a sum (the step above) and compare.
y-m-34-09.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The leading term of A·B is ..., so ...
y-m-34-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you show that the leading coefficient of the product is the product of the two coefficients, ab?
y-m-34-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use the point that a≠0 and b≠0, so ab≠0?
y-m-34-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state the difference that in a sum, coefficients of the same degree are added and can become 0?
y-m-34-09.s.s3.model.0: The leading term of A·B is ax³·bx³=abx⁶, and since a and b are not 0, ab is not 0 either. So the x⁶ term remains and the degree is 6. In a sum, coefficients of the same degree are added and can become 0, so the term disappears, but in a product the coefficients are multiplied and do not become 0.
y-m-34-09.s.s3.model.1: In a product, the x⁶ term is made by only one thing, the product of the leading terms, so no other term can cancel it. Its coefficient ab is not 0 because a and b are not 0. In a sum, terms can cancel each other and disappear, like 2x³ and -2x³.

y-m-34-10.title: Explaining to a friend when the x coefficient of the dividing linear expression is 2
y-m-34-10.topic: The remainder theorem: the remainder and quotient when the coefficient of the linear expression is not 1
y-m-34-10.goal: Find the error that arose in a solution note when the divisor's coefficient is not 1, judge how the quotient and remainder change, and then fix the explanation so a friend can follow it.
y-m-34-10.material: The following is part of an explanation note written by a student. f(x) is a polynomial.
y-m-34-10.thinking.1: Judging how the quotient and remainder change
y-m-34-10.thinking.2: Fixing the explanation with the reader in mind
y-m-34-10.prereq.0: Assumption: H3 (difficulty level 3) of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment; it does not mean an education authority assigned it to a particular grade. Students are assumed to have already learned polynomial operations at the level of high school Common Math.
y-m-34-10.prereq.2: The fact that the remainder when dividing by a linear expression is a constant
y-m-34-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in this note that went off.
y-m-34-10.s.s1.hint.0: As you read each line, check whether the rule obtained in the earlier lines was carried over as is into the expression in the last line.
y-m-34-10.s.s1.hint.1: In the last line, find yourself the 'x that makes the divisor 0'.
y-m-34-10.s.s1.line.0: If the quotient when f(x) is divided by x-3 is Q(x) and the remainder is R, then f(x)=(x-3)Q(x)+R.
y-m-34-10.s.s1.line.1: The divisor is a linear expression, so the remainder R is a constant.
y-m-34-10.s.s1.line.2: Plugging in x=3 makes (x-3)Q(x)=0, so f(3)=R.
y-m-34-10.s.s1.line.3: In the same way, the remainder when f(x) is divided by 2x-6 is f(6), the value with x=6.
y-m-34-10.s.s1.explain: The 4th line went off. The x that makes 2x-6=0 is 3, not 6. The 3rd line said to plug in the x that makes the divisor 0. For 2x-6 you have to plug in x=3, so the remainder is f(3).
y-m-34-10.s.s2.prompt: When the quotient of f(x) divided by x-3 is Q(x) and the remainder is R, what are the quotient and remainder when f(x) is divided by 2x-6?
y-m-34-10.s.s2.hint.0: In f(x)=(x-3)Q(x)+R, rewrite (x-3) in a product form that contains 2x-6.
y-m-34-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the degree of the remainder is less than the degree of the divisor.
y-m-34-10.s.s2.r.a: (2x-6)·2Q(x)=4(x-3)Q(x), so it differs from the original expression.
y-m-34-10.s.s2.r.b: The remainder is f(3) regardless of the coefficient of the divisor. There is no reason to change the remainder to half.
y-m-34-10.s.s2.r.c: This judgment sees the quotient as unchanged even though the divisor doubled. (2x-6)Q(x) is twice (x-3)Q(x).
y-m-34-10.s.s2.r.d: You chose it using the fact that (x-3)Q(x) can be written as (2x-6)·(Q(x)/2).
y-m-34-10.s.s2.explain: f(x)=(x-3)Q(x)+R=(2x-6)·(Q(x)/2)+R, and R is a constant, so it satisfies the degree condition. So the quotient when dividing by 2x-6 is Q(x)/2 and the remainder stays R.
y-m-34-10.s.s3.prompt: Fix the 4th line and explain it to a friend who has just started learning math. Write what the remainder is when dividing by 2x-6 and how you can know it, so the friend can follow along.
y-m-34-10.s.s3.hint.0: First find the value of x that makes 2x-6 equal 0.
y-m-34-10.s.s3.hint.1: Write which term disappears when you plug that value of x into the form f(x)=(2x-6)·(quotient)+(remainder).
y-m-34-10.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The remainder when dividing by 2x-6 is ... This is because ...
y-m-34-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say why it must be x=3 and not x=6, in terms of 'the value that makes the divisor 0'?
y-m-34-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write it in an order a friend can follow (set up the equation, find x, plug in)?
y-m-34-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you point out that the quotient changes but the remainder is the same?
y-m-34-10.s.s3.model.0: The remainder when dividing by 2x-6 is also f(3). The x that makes 2x-6=0 is 3, so plugging x=3 into f(x)=(2x-6)Q(x)+R makes (2x-6)Q(x) equal 0, so f(3)=R. You don't plug in x=6.
y-m-34-10.s.s3.model.1: f(x)=(x-3)Q(x)+R can also be written as (2x-6)·(Q(x)/2)+R, so the remainder R stays the same and only the quotient becomes half. So the remainder when dividing by 2x-6 is also f(3).
